paragraphs: After the great war of Kurukshetra, the five Pandava brothers held a magnificent sacrifice and showered the poor with lavish gifts. Everyone agreed the world had never seen anything like it. Then, when the ceremony was over, a small mongoose appeared. Half of its body was golden and the other half brown. It rolled about on the floor of the hall and declared that everyone there was lying: this was no sacrifice at all.
The people were outraged. Hadn't money and jewels poured out until every poor person was rich and happy? The mongoose answered with a story.

In a small village there once lived a poor Brahmin with his wife, his son and his son's wife. They survived on small offerings given for teaching and preaching. Then a famine struck that lasted three years, and the family went hungry for days on end. One morning the father managed to get hold of a little barley flour. They divided it into four portions and cooked it. Just as they sat down to eat, someone knocked. At the door stood a guest, and in India a guest is honoured as if he were a god.

The Brahmin welcomed him and gave him his own share. The guest gulped it down and said it had only sharpened his hunger after ten days of starving. The wife offered her portion. Her husband refused, but she insisted it was their duty to feed a guest, and hers to give when he had nothing left. The guest ate it and was still burning with hunger. The son gave his share, saying a son should help his father keep his duty. Still the guest was not satisfied, so the son's wife gave hers too. At last the guest was content, and he left blessing them.

That night all four died of hunger. A few grains of their flour had fallen on the floor, said the mongoose, and when it rolled on them, half its body turned to gold. Ever since, it had wandered the world looking for another sacrifice like that one. It had never found one. Its other half was still brown.

Swamiji added that this spirit of giving was fading. He recalled an English schoolbook that spent pages praising a boy for giving some of his wages to his mother, something any Indian boy would simply take for granted. Where people live only for themselves while their families are left to suffer, he said, that can never be the ideal of a householder.
learn: The value of a gift isn't measured by its size but by what it costs the giver. Sharing your time, food or attention when you have little to spare means more than a showy donation. And caring for family is a duty, not a favour.
